newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French 10-year bond futures settled in positive territory but off their peaks on Thursday after coming under selling pressure late in the day on the back of losses by U.S. Treasuries.

They continued to lose ground in after-hours trade in what analysts said was a reaction to negative U.S. housing data. U.S. existing home sales surged in February, fuelling worries that the economy was overheating and that it might prompt further rate hikes.
"We were doing fine until the housing data. Now the market is crumbling," said one bond future trader.

Trading was quiet most of the day ahead of the four-day Easter holiday weekend starting on Friday with investors staying on the sidelines, not wishing to take positions, especially with next week's expected raft of U.S. data.
The French market will be closed on Monday when U.S. NAPM figures are released.
After hitting a high of 128.42, the notionnel retraced to settle up 0.08 basis points at 128.28. It then fell in after-hours trade to 127.86 by 1725 GMT, hit by the selloff of U.S. Treasuries.
But PIBOR performed strongly, buoyed by non-resident purchases, as the franc fell below 3.37 francs permark to trade at 3.3695/98 against 3.3710/13 on Wednesday.

"PIBOR is not expensive and a lot of people are starting to say if the U.S. economy is overheating, it will need more than a 25 basis point rise in the Fed funds rate to hose it down, with all the risks that could have for the T-bond and to a lesser extent the long end of the European curve," said one analyst.
"By contrast, the short end of the European curve looks well protected," he said.
Nathalie Fillet, Paribas analyst, said the latest weak French data on consumption and business prospects "prove the European and U.S. economies are in completely different phases.

But while prospects for the French short end appeared positive, one trader said the long end was likely to suffer further in the coming week ahead of key U.S. payrolls data due on Friday. "I think there's a risk of going lower," he said.

"The only thing supporting the long European end is that speculators are a bit nervous about shorting it. But we're in a typical wait-and-see market. Even if there is a lot of liquidity, investors keep on looking for excuses not to buy."
He said the reluctance to buy had led to "a semi-paralysis of the primary market where a lot of issues in the pipeline have been delayed".
The decision, as expected, by the Bank of France to leave key interest rates unchanged after a meeting of its monetary policy council on Thursday, had no market impact, dealers said.

A majority of economists polled by Reuters on Wednesday said they did not see the Bank of France cutting the key intervention rate this week, nor or in the coming weeks, but that they still believed rates could come down slightly further in France.
